title: Pride and Prejudice . . . and Other Blind Spots
coreMove: Treat your own certainty as one perspective to inspect, not the neutral place from which everyone else is judged.
sourcePressure: The chapter moves from dissonance into naive realism, bias blind spots, and prejudice; the source stresses that people experience their own view as reality while seeing the opponent as distorted.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Turning blind spots into a lecture about other people's prejudice rather than the felt innocence of one's own perception.

sourceAnchors.name: bias blind spot
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names the habit of noticing bias in others more readily than in oneself
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The bias blind spot is most dangerous when you feel unusually fair, because that feeling becomes part of the shield.

sourceAnchors.name: naive realism
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports the claim that one's own perception can feel like direct reality rather than an interpretation
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Naive realism is the quiet conviction that you are not interpreting the scene; you are simply seeing it.

hook: Do not start with red-team versus blue-team politics.
Avoid a generic argument at Thanksgiving.
counterintuition: Do not make the lesson "everyone is biased" and stop there.
tryThisNow: No broad perspective-taking exercise without evidence.
examples: No social-media feed as default shell.
No classroom debate as the main repeated setting.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective realization, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: a hiring panel reviewing two candidates after a structured interview
exampleSpecs.audience: managers who believe their gut read is unusually objective
exampleSpecs.stakes: a qualified candidate gets discounted because the panel treats confidence as neutrality
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Claire writes each panelist's first impression beside the scorecard criterion before anyone can call their favorite simply "a better fit"
exampleSpecs.firstImage: two clipped scorecards under a glass conference-room nameplate

exampleSpecs.domain: a condo board noise dispute between an upstairs pianist and a downstairs shift worker
exampleSpecs.audience: neighbors whose own inconvenience feels like the whole truth
exampleSpecs.stakes: the board may punish one resident while never testing its own assumptions
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Julien asks both residents to mark the same week on a sound log before labeling either person unreasonable
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a decibel meter case beside a stack of condo bylaws

exampleSpecs.domain: a newsroom correction meeting after a local profile framed a neighborhood group as obstructionist
exampleSpecs.audience: editors who treat their framing as facts
exampleSpecs.stakes: the paper repeats a stereotype while insisting it is simply being realistic
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It takes Anke reading the unused interview notes aloud to show how the article selected only the quotes that fit the obstruction frame
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stack of annotated interview transcripts under a blue copy desk lamp

exampleSpecs.domain: a youth rugby referee committee reviewing parent complaints after a regional final
exampleSpecs.audience: volunteers sorting disputed calls under loyalty pressure
exampleSpecs.stakes: the committee may protect its own club by calling the rival parents biased
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: David predicts which complaints came from his club, then opens the anonymized clips and sees his accuracy collapse
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a whistle cord tangled around a tablet showing paused match footage

exampleSpecs.domain: a scholarship committee reading essays from urban and rural applicants
exampleSpecs.audience: reviewers who see themselves as fair but carry a narrow picture of promise
exampleSpecs.stakes: the committee may reward familiarity while calling it merit
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Isabel cover names and schools, then list which details she had been treating as ambition rather than mere familiarity
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a pile of anonymized essays held by a brass binder clip

exampleSpecs.domain: a product design review for a banking app used by elderly customers
exampleSpecs.audience: designers who confuse their own fluent use with obvious use
exampleSpecs.stakes: older users keep abandoning bill pay while the team blames resistance to change
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Chidi watches a recorded session with the interface labels blurred, then changes the team's claim from "users are confused" to "our path hides the next step"
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a tablet on a stand with oversized checkout text taped over the screen edge

skillTargets: recognize when objectivity feels like proof but is only perspective
choose tests that expose the observer's own filtering
analyze how prejudice can survive inside a fair self-image

tryThisNowSpec: Before your next disagreement, write one sentence beginning "My read may be shaped by..." and fill it with a concrete loyalty, fear, or prior commitment.
